streets.direction: from the top of the Velia (Arch of Titus site) to the Forum
streets.notes: P-A: the 'Sacra via' of the sources is only the stretch from the Velia to the Regia (the common but wrong extension to the Colosseum and across the Forum to the Capitol is modern usage); the line shown continues to the Forum floor at the east end of the Basilica Aemilia. The bend north of the later temple of Divus Iulius is the Augustan line (after 36 BC); before that the street ran straighter to the Regia and Vesta. Nero changed the line east of the arch of Titus (outside our period).
sources: Platner-Ashby s.v. Sacra Via (read): from the summit of the Velia, where it passed near the temple of Jupiter Stator and the later arch of Titus, down to the east end of the Forum by the Regia; a fornix Fabianus spanned it from 121 BC; Sullan-period pavement found at 11.90-12.50 m a.s.l. near the temple of Caesar, c. 14 m at the 'temple of Romulus', c. 27 m at the Clivus Palatinus
Cic. pro Planc. 17
Hor. Sat. 1.9.1
Livy 41.27.5 (paving of the city streets, 174 BC)
streets.width_source: P-A s.v. Sacra Via: Augustan pavement 5 m wide

streets.direction: from the west corner of the Forum, past the temple of Saturn, up to the Asylum / Capitol
streets.notes: Upper course lost (P-A: no trace of the upper part or the branch to the Arx); the end point at the Asylum is the line P-A gives, the last turn toward the temple of Jupiter is conjecture.
sources: Platner-Ashby s.v. Clivus Capitolinus (read): a path continuing the Sacra via, made a cart road at the end of the regal period; paved in 174 BC by the censors Fulvius Flaccus and Postumius Albinus; starts near the corner of the Basilica Iulia, skirts the north front and west side of the temple of Saturn, ascends to the Asylum with a gradient of about 1:8
Livy 41.27.7 (paved with silex, 174 BC)
Livy 37.3 (Scipio's arch at the top, 190 BC)
Cic. pro Mil. 64 (houses on the clivus)

streets.direction: from the Forum between Curia and Carcer, along the Capitoline slope toward the Campus Martius
streets.notes: The name Clivus Argentarius is found only in medieval documents (P-A); we use it for the Republican street. Ends at the Porta Fontinalis, where Via Lata begins.
sources: Platner-Ashby s.v. Clivus Argentarius (read): the only immediate connection between the Forum and the Campus Martius before the imperial fora; left the Forum between the curia and the carcer and ran along the slope of the Capitol, corresponding to the modern Via di Marforio; in the Republic it seems to have been called Lautumiae
Platner-Ashby s.v. Vicus Iugarius (read): 'the road which preceded the via Flaminia and the clivus Argentarius'

streets.direction: from the Forum between the Basilica Iulia and the temple of Castor, south along the west flank of the Palatine to the Forum Boarium
sources: Platner-Ashby s.v. Vicus Tuscus (read): principal artery between the Forum and the Forum Boarium and Circus Maximus; the eastern boundary of the Velabrum; shops of silk, incense, perfume, clothing; pavement of small brick cubes found between the Basilica Iulia and the temple of Castor
Livy 27.37.15 and 33.26.9 (the route of the procession)
Dion. Hal. 5.36.4

streets.direction: from the Forum between the Basilica Iulia and the temple of Castor, west along the foot of the Capitol to the Porta Carmentalis
streets.notes: Part of the original trade route from the north and east to the Tiber crossing below the island (P-A).
sources: Platner-Ashby s.v. Vicus Iugarius (read): led from the Forum, between the Basilica Iulia and the temple of Castor, to the Porta Carmentalis, 'kept close to the southern edge of the Capitol'; before the Augustan period it lay a little further south-east

streets.direction: from the Vicus Iugarius south through the Velabrum past the later church of S. Giorgio to the Forum Boarium
streets.english: Street through the Velabrum to the Forum Boarium
streets.notes: The Velabrum was drained by the Cloaca Maxima; no ancient name or line is attested for a street across it. This is a reconstruction joining the Vicus Iugarius to the Forum Boarium at the Arcus Argentariorum, as the owner asked ('the street through the Velabrum to the Forum Boarium'). Treat as rough.
sources: Platner-Ashby s.v. Velabrum (read): the district lay between the vicus Tuscus on the east and the vicus Iugarius on the west; the dividing line between Velabrum and Forum Boarium passes S. Giorgio in Velabro and the arcus Argentariorum; 'all the traffic between the forum and the pons Sublicius passed through the streets that bounded it'
Platner-Ashby s.v. Forum Boarium (read)

streets.direction: from the Forum between Curia and Basilica Aemilia north-east to the Subura
sources: Platner-Ashby s.v. Argiletum (read): the street between the Subura and the Forum, entered between the Curia and the Basilica Aemilia; its lower part, occupied by private houses (Cic. Att. 1.14.7; 12.32.2), later became the Forum Transitorium
Livy 1.19.2
Mart. 1.3.1 (booksellers)

streets.direction: from the head of the Argiletum east up the Subura valley between Viminal and Oppius (modern Via della Madonna dei Monti / Via Cavour)
sources: Platner-Ashby s.v. Subura (read): the valley between the southern end of the Viminal and the Oppius, connected with the Forum by the Argiletum and continued east between the Oppius and the Cispius by the Clivus Suburanus to the Porta Esquilina; now traversed by Via Cavour and Via dello Statuto
Mart. 2.17; 12.18.2 (clamosa); Juv. 11.51 (fervens)

streets.direction: from the Subura east between the Oppius and the Cispius to the Porta Esquilina
streets.notes: No separate P-A article online (# unverified for details); the line follows the modern Via di S. Martino ai Monti / Via di S. Pietro in Vincoli valley as a guess.
sources: Platner-Ashby s.v. Subura (read): continued eastward 'by the Clivus Suburanus, ending at the Porta Esquilina'
Platner-Ashby s.v. Regiones Quattuordecim (read): the clivus Suburanus from the porta Esquilina west bounds Regions III and IV
Platner-Ashby s.v. Via Praenestina (read): the Clivus Suburanus led to the Porta Esquilina

streets.direction: from the Subura north-east between the Cispius and the Viminal (modern Via Urbana) to the Porta Viminalis
sources: Platner-Ashby s.v. Subura (read): 'a third depression north-east between the Cispius and the Viminal that was marked by the vicus Patricius'
Platner-Ashby s.v. Regiones Quattuordecim (read): the vicus Patricius from the porta Viminalis to a point near the Subura bounds Region IV
Via Urbana (S. Pudenziana in vico Patricii) as the modern equivalent: # unverified

streets.direction: from the Subura / Argiletum north-east up the valley between Quirinal and Viminal (area of Via Nazionale) to the Alta Semita
streets.notes: No separate P-A article online. The owner's brief places it in the Via Nazionale area; the real line is disputed and the points are a conjectural valley road. Treat as rough.
sources: Platner-Ashby s.v. Vicus Iugarius (read): the via Salaria, the vicus Longus, the clivus Insteius and the Argiletum formed one of the routes from the north-east to the Tiber crossing
Platner-Ashby s.v. Subura (read): a depression extended from the Subura northward between the Viminal and the Quirinal

streets.direction: north-east along the ridge of the Quirinal (modern Via del Quirinale, Via XX Settembre) to the Porta Collina
sources: Platner-Ashby s.v. Alta Semita (read): the principal street of Region VI, ran north-east along the ridge of the Quirinal to the porta Collina, corresponding with the modern Via del Quirinale and Via Venti Settembre; ancient pavement 1.83 m below the present level; the north-east part probably called Vicus portae Collinae
Platner-Ashby s.v. Regiones Quattuordecim (read)

streets.direction: from the Sacra via at the north-east corner of the Palatine, along the north slope of the hill to the Velabrum
streets.notes: P-A: the original road may have lain a little north of the excavated imperial line.
sources: Platner-Ashby s.v. Nova Via (read): began near the temple of Jupiter Stator, ran along the north slope of the Palatine between the aedes Vestae and the lucus Vestae (Cic. Div. 1.101) to the north-west corner and the Velabrum (Varro LL 6.24; 5.43); excavated pavement at 23.40 m above sea level behind the atrium Vestae and 32.30 m at the Clivus Palatinus
Livy 1.41.4
Varro LL 6.59

streets.direction: from the Sacra via near the arch of Titus up to the Porta Mugonia and the Palatine
streets.notes: No separate P-A article online (# unverified); P-A calls it 'so-called'. Short stub only.
sources: Platner-Ashby s.v. Sacra Via (read): the so-called clivus Palatinus branched off south from the Sacra via near the arch of Titus and ascended the Palatine at the porta Mugonia; junction at about 27.6 m above sea level
Platner-Ashby s.v. Nova Via (read)

streets.direction: from the Porta Fontinalis on the east slope of the Capitol north across the Campus Martius (modern Via del Corso) to the Porta Flaminia site; then on to the Pons Mulvius
streets.english: Broad Way (Flaminian Way in the city)
streets.latin: Via Lata (Via Flaminia inside the walls)
streets.notes: Inside the Aurelian walls (to about 41.9108) the points follow the modern Corso (P-A: coincides absolutely) so are approx; beyond Porta Flaminia they are rough. Before 220 BC the Prata Flaminia and Campus were open ground with only tracks. Before it was paved the Via Flaminia outside the city was gravelled; inside the city paved from 174 BC (Livy 41.27.5).
sources: Platner-Ashby s.v. Via Flaminia (read): built 220 BC by the censor C. Flaminius (Livy Per. 20); starts from a gate of the Servian wall on the east slope of the Capitol; ran across the Campus Martius 'in an absolutely straight line to the pons Mulvius'; 'the modern Corso coincides absolutely with the ancient line'
Platner-Ashby s.v. Via Lata: the name for the intramural part is attested only from the 4th c. AD
Livy Per. 20

streets.direction: from the Campus Martius south between the Capitol and the river, through the Porta Carmentalis and Porta Flumentana, to the Porta Trigemina
streets.english: Road along the Tiber side of the Capitol to the Forum Boarium and Porta Trigemina
streets.latin: Road from the Campus Martius through the Porta Carmentalis (name not attested)
sources: Platner-Ashby s.v. Forum Boarium (read): 'the road which ran from the campus Martius between the Capitol and the river, passing through the porta Carmentalis and the porta Flumentana, and on to the porta Trigemina'
Platner-Ashby s.v. Vicus Iugarius (read)

streets.direction: from the valley of the Circus Maximus up the Aventine
streets.notes: No separate P-A article online (# unverified). The date 238 BC rests on the Publicii's aedileship as I recall it from Ovid and Varro; treat as probable.
sources: Platner-Ashby s.v. Forum Boarium (read): mentions 'the clivus Publicius descending from the' Aventine to the road along the valley of the Circus Maximus
Ovid Fasti 5.275-294 (the aediles L. and M. Publicius Malleolus built it from fines, 238 BC): # unverified, from memory; Livy 41.27.5 for paving

streets.direction: from the Porta Capena south-east (modern Via di Porta S. Sebastiano) to the site of the Aurelian Porta Appia, one Roman mile out
streets.latin: Via Appia (first mile, Porta Capena to the later Porta Appia)
streets.notes: Split from the outer road at the Aurelian Porta Appia (about one mile from the Porta Capena), because the two parts were paved in different years (189 and 293 BC). P-A: this part of the course ran a little further north-east than the modern Via di Porta S. Sebastiano.
sources: Platner-Ashby s.v. Via Appia (read): built 312 BC by the censor Appius Claudius Caecus (Livy 9.29); issued from the Porta Capena; 'the original road was only gravelled'; in 296 a footpath saxo quadrato from the gate to the templum Martis (Livy 10.23.12); in 189 B.C. the first mile, from the gate to the temple, was paved with silex (Livy 38.28.3)
Livy 38.28.3 (read, Latin Library): uiam silice sternendam a porta Capena ad Martis locauerunt
Platner-Ashby: the first milestone was just inside the porta Appia

streets.direction: from the first mile south-east along the modern Via Appia Antica
streets.english: Appian Way beyond the first mile
streets.notes: Gravel (glareo strata) from 312 to 293 BC, paved from 293 (Livy 10.47.4, three years after the footpath of 296). Beyond about 1.5 km from the gate the points are rough.
sources: Platner-Ashby s.v. Via Appia (read): three years after the 296 footpath the whole road was paved with silex from the temple of Mars to Bovillae (Livy 10.47.4)
Livy 10.47.4 (read, Latin Library): via a Martis silice ad Bovillas perstrata est

streets.direction: branches left from the Via Appia about 830 m beyond the Porta Capena, through the later Porta Latina, south-east
streets.notes: Not attested as paved within 509-27 BC in the sources we read; shown as gravel. exists_from -334 is the latest safe 'it is there' date (P-A: 'at least as early as 334').
sources: Platner-Ashby s.v. Via Latina (read): branched off the Appia 830 m from the porta Capena and 500 m further passed the Porta Latina; an artificial military highway, probably built after 389 BC and in existence as far as Cales by 334 (Livy 10.36)
Livy 10.36

streets.direction: from the Porta Trigemina along the north-west and south-west sides of the Aventine, then south (modern Via Marmorata, Via Ostiense)
streets.notes: Beyond the tomb of Cestius (41.8760, 12.4812) the points are rough.
sources: Platner-Ashby s.v. Via Ostiensis (read): the road from the Porta Trigemina 'kept under the north-west and south-west sides of the Aventine', joined by branches from the Porta Lavernalis and Porta Raudusculana a little beyond the tomb of Cestius; then due south; 14 miles to Ostia; archaic milestone set up by the aediles
Livy 41.27.5 (the Emporium outside the Porta Trigemina paved with stone, 174 BC)

streets.direction: north from the Porta Collina (modern Via Salaria begins at the Aurelian Porta Salaria)
sources: Platner-Ashby s.v. Via Salaria (read): a very ancient road, by which the Sabines fetched salt from the marshes at the mouth of the Tiber (Festus 326; Strabo 5.3.1); passed through the porta Collina, and the via Nomentana left it immediately outside the gate
Livy 7.9.6

streets.direction: from just outside the Porta Collina north-east (Via Ficulensis) to the later Porta Nomentana and Nomentum
sources: Platner-Ashby s.v. Via Nomentana (read): diverged immediately outside the porta Collina from the via Salaria; originally led to Ficulea (Livy 3.52, via Ficulensis), then prolonged to Nomentum, 14 miles; a road of purely local importance

streets.direction: from the Porta Esquilina east-north-east to Tibur
streets.notes: P-A hedges on the start; the Esquilina start is chosen.
sources: Platner-Ashby s.v. Via Tiburtina (read): 'probably left the city by the porta Esquilina of the Servian wall' (other theories use the Porta Viminalis); 20 miles to Tibur, becoming the Via Valeria beyond

streets.direction: from the Porta Esquilina east to the Porta Praenestina (Porta Maggiore) and on to Gabii and Praeneste
streets.notes: The intramural stretch (Porta Esquilina to the Aurelian Porta Praenestina) is shared with the Via Labicana: P-A s.v. Via Labicana says the intramural road from the Porta Esquilina 'should really bear the same name'. It is drawn once, here.
sources: Platner-Ashby s.v. Via Praenestina (read): began at the porta Esquilina (to which the Clivus Suburanus led) and separated from the via Labicana just before the Porta Praenestina; pavement and the 'Casa Tonda' found at Piazza Vittorio Emanuele; originally the Via Gabina to Gabii, then prolonged to Praeneste (25 miles)

streets.direction: from the Porta Praenestina junction south-east to Labici
sources: Platner-Ashby s.v. Via Labicana (read): diverged to the right from the via Praenestina just inside the porta Praenestina of the Aurelian wall; the first part may have belonged to the original route to Tusculum; ran to Labici, 15 miles

streets.direction: from the pons Aemilius across Trastevere and up the Janiculum, then west
streets.notes: The pons Aemilius was built 179/142 BC (see monuments.yaml); before the bridge the Trastevere road started at the Pons Sublicius. The points use the later bridge.
sources: Platner-Ashby s.v. Via Aurelia (read): 'the road which led from the pons Aemilius across the low ground on the right bank of the Tiber (two arches of a viaduct found near S. Crisogono) up to the Janiculum, where it passed through the Aurelian wall by the Porta Aurelia'
date of the road (a consul Aurelius Cotta, c. 241 BC): # unverified, not in the P-A article we read
